title: Borscht
subtitle: Eastern European beetroot soup with soured cream
excerpt: A vivid deep-crimson soup of beetroot, cabbage, and potato in a lightly tangy broth, served hot with a swirl of soured cream. The signature dish of Ukrainian and Russian cooking.

recipe.sourceNotes: Borscht is the national dish of Ukraine and is found across Eastern Europe and the former Soviet states in many versions. Ukrainian borscht, often considered the original and most complex version, typically contains beetroot, cabbage, potatoes, carrots, tomatoes, onion, garlic, and sometimes pork or beef. The addition of vinegar or sour cream gives it its characteristic slight tanginess. Borscht can be served hot or cold: the cold (chilled) version is especially associated with Polish and Ashkenazi Jewish cooking. The deep crimson colour comes from the beetroot and is susceptible to pH: an acidic element (vinegar or sour cream) keeps it bright red; an alkaline environment turns it brown.

content.text: Add a splash of vinegar or lemon juice at the end of cooking to brighten the colour and flavour: without it the soup can look and taste slightly flat. The beetroot can be cooked two ways: grated raw into the pot or pre-roasted and diced. The grated raw version gives the most intense colour; roasted gives a sweeter, more complex flavour. Do not rush the initial cook: the colour needs time to develop. Taste for balance before serving: borscht should be sweet from the beetroot, sour from the vinegar, and savoury from the broth.
Heat the oil in a large pot over medium heat. Cook the onion for 8 minutes until soft and golden. Add the carrot and cook for 5 minutes. Add the garlic and tomato puree and stir for 2 minutes.
Add the grated beetroot and stir to coat in the tomato base. Pour in the stock and add the bay leaves. Season. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook for 20 minutes.
Add the potato and cabbage. Simmer for a further 20 to 25 minutes until the potato is completely tender.

Add the vinegar. Taste and adjust: add more vinegar for more tartness, more salt if needed. Remove the bay leaves. Ladle into bowls. Top each with a generous spoonful of soured cream and a scatter of chopped parsley.
